extracted.intended_audience: PR and communications professionals, marketers, startup founders, and anyone who pitches journalists/editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting short, personalized email pitches to journalists and editors to propose story ideas and earn media coverage. Focuses on subject lines, personalization, structure, timing, follow-up, and common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject line: Make it irresistible
rubrics_metrics.description: This is your first (and sometimes only) chance to grab attention. Journalists scan their inboxes quickly, so your subject line needs to be clear, specific, and intriguing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it doesn’t make them open the email, the rest of your pitch won’t matter. Use short, specific subject lines that promise value or a news peg (e.g., “Exclusive: New App Cuts Wasted Meeting Time by 30%”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization: Know your journalist
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass emails get ignored. A pitch should clearly show you’ve done your homework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention the journalist’s recent work, align your idea with their beat, or explain why the audience will care. Personalization demonstrates respect and increases response likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hook: Lead with the story angle
rubrics_metrics.description: The first line should deliver the 'why now.' Don’t bury the lead; get straight to the story idea and make it clear why it matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with a compelling angle or news peg so the journalist immediately understands relevance and timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting details: Keep it concise and relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: After the hook, add just enough context to back it up. This might be a stat, a quote, or a short explainer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide essentials only—enough so the journalist knows what to expect, but not the full backstory. Concrete evidence (metrics, quotes) strengthens credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: CTA: What do you want the journalist to do?
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a clear next step, such as scheduling an interview or getting in touch with you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make it easy for them to say yes by telling them exactly what you’re offering and how to act on it (e.g., interview, demo, early access, full dataset).

rubrics_metrics.name: Research your target media outlet
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you write a single word, know who you’re pitching. Look into the outlet’s audience, tone, and content style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand whether the outlet publishes hard news, human interest, or thought leadership and align your pitch to that format to increase odds of being noticed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor the pitch to the journalist's beat
rubrics_metrics.description: Many publications have multiple editors/journalists covering specific topics; choose the editor who covers your topic area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check recent articles and the outlet’s media kit or editor page. Don’t pitch a marketing trend to a health reporter; a well-matched pitch shows respect and improves response chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft your email (length and structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep your pitch short and focused, 3-4 paragraphs max. Start with a strong subject line and an attention-grabbing hook, briefly explain your story idea and finish with a clear CTA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the email skimmable: short paragraphs, bullet points where useful. Example structure: subject, personalized opener, hook/angle, 1–2 supporting details, CTA. Avoid long blocks of text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow up professionally (timing and tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you don’t hear back after 3–5 business days, a polite follow-up is fair game.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep follow-ups brief (a quick 'just checking in'), restate value from the original email, and offer to answer questions. Persistence is acceptable, but don't be pushy—if you still don’t get a response, move on.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to send (best and worst times)
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing of sending is as important as content: mid-week (Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Thursdays) and early to mid-morning (8:30–11:30 AM) tend to perform best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid Mondays and Fridays, late afternoons (2:00–6:00 PM), weekends, and holidays. Mid-morning mid-week increases the chance your email gets read rather than buried.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being too promotional
rubrics_metrics.description: Media pitches aren’t advertisements. Journalists don’t want to promote brands—they want to share stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus the pitch on the value, angle, or newsworthy element, not overtly promoting the product or company. Treat editorial interest as the priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid generic copy-paste emails
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s okay to use a pitch template, but make sure it doesn’t look like a mass email when you send it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic templates come off as insincere and rarely show the journalist you know their beat. Always personalize before sending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness / clear angle required
rubrics_metrics.description: If there’s no hook, there’s no story. Always lead with what makes your pitch relevant and timely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate why the topic matters now and why the outlet’s audience should care. Without newsworthiness, journalists are unlikely to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the pitch skimmable and offer value fast
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer value fast and make the pitch easy to skim with short paragraphs and bullet points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists process many emails—lead with the most important info and format to enable quick scanning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer assets and concrete next steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell journalists exactly what you can provide (e.g., interview, demo, data set, early access).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offering assets like demos or data and being explicit about availability makes it easier for journalists to accept and act on the pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tools to improve pitching strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Use media pitching tools, CRMs, and alerts to identify relevant journalists, monitor opens/responses, and automate follow-ups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Meltwater for locating journalists and tracking outreach, CRMs for tracking leads from earned media, and Google Alerts for finding journalists covering your keywords. Tools can save time and increase targeting accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended pitch length
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for a pitch that is long enough to get the point across but short enough to skim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence boundary: be persistent but not pushy
rubrics_metrics.description: Persistence is fine, but pushiness kills relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no reply after a polite follow-up or two, move on rather than repeatedly emailing; maintain professional tone to preserve relationships for future opportunities.
